evidence: In January 2025 the Georgia PSC unanimously approved a rule letting Georgia Power apply special billing terms to new customers of 100 MW or more; it covers Georgia Power only, not EMCs or municipal utilities.
pending: Rule does not reach EMCs/munis; legislative bills for a statutory large-load class (SB 34/SB 410) did not pass in 2026.

evidence: The PSC rule allows minimum monthly bills and extends contract terms from 5 to 15 years for 100 MW+ customers so Georgia Power recovers costs if a customer leaves.
pending: Exact minimum-bill percentage not found in sources.

evidence: Large-load customers must pay transmission and distribution costs as construction progresses and new contracts go to the PSC at least 30 days before signing; no specific $/MW deposit figure found.

PSC orders (April 2024 order, January 2025 rule) require Georgia Power to show data center revenue does not raise residential bills and to file cost-allocation studies so large loads pay their cost of service.
pending: Statutory ratepayer-protection language (SB 34 folded into SB 410) did not become law; critics say PSC rule is not strong enough.

evidence: Democratic gubernatorial nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms has called for a pause on new data centers; statewide moratorium bills failed in the 2026 session, while 12+ local jurisdictions have temporary moratoria.
pending: Pledge becomes actionable only if Bottoms is confirmed governor-elect (election result not verified in sources I could open); legislature and Kemp-era Republican control may block it. Local moratoria in DeKalb, Cobb, Clayton and others expire late 2026.

evidence: Georgia has no state siting board for data centers; siting is decided by local zoning, with counties adopting their own ordinances and setbacks.
The only state-level extra review is the PSC requirement that Georgia Power contracts with customers above 100 MW be filed for PSC review before execution.
No fast-track or backlog program documented for data center permits; feasibility is constrained by utility interconnection timelines and capacity.

Georgia's data center sales-tax exemption remains in effect after the 2026 House left it out of the repeal package, ending Senate Bill 410; a state audit estimated the foregone revenue at $474 million for 2025.
pending: Kemp vetoed a 2024 pause (HB 1192); a Bottoms administration or new legislature could revisit; SB 410 would have ended exemptions after honoring existing ones through 2028 and 2031.

evidence: Local development authorities routinely offer property-tax abatements to data centers.
The exemption is tied to minimum investment/job thresholds set in statute, but I found no evidence of strict clawbacks; critics (Sen. Parent, Sierra Club) note weak protections.
No state data-center water limits or reporting found; only local proposals such as Atlanta's special-use-permit disclosure of estimated water and energy use.
No Georgia-specific generator rules found; advocacy groups are asking for Tier 4 controls and a cumulative-impact study, implying only baseline permitting today.
No data-center-specific state environmental review found.
No state curtailment, demand-response or on-site-generation rule specific to data centers found.
No prevailing-wage or local-hire mandate for data centers found.
Georgia Power must file quarterly reports on new data centers with the PSC, but there is no operator-level public energy/water reporting statute.
Noise and setback rules (e.g., 100-ft residential setbacks) are local, not statewide.
About 20 data center bills failed in 2026, the gubernatorial race centers on data centers, and PSC load-growth and cost-allocation proceedings (including the OpenAI deal review) remain active.
pending: Bottoms pause pledge; possible 2027 repeal/clawback of tax exemption; Georgia Power large-load contract reviews.

evidence: Georgia Power's projected data center load rose from 400 MW to 8,500 MW in a few years and the PSC allowed 6,000 MW (up to 8,500 MW) of new generation, indicating capacity and interconnection constraints.

SB 484 (effective July 1, 2026) requires every public utility to file a large-load tariff by October 1, 2026 for single-site loads of 50 MW or more; FPL says its PSC-approved 2026-2029 rate structure already complies and the PSC must review it.
pending: PSC review of utility compliance tariffs (due Oct 1, 2026); a separate report says regulators rejected Duke Energy Florida's data center rate structure.

evidence: FPL's large-load terms require a 20-year minimum contract with exit fees, and SB 484 lets the PSC approve minimum demand charges, take-or-pay and early termination fees.
SB 484 lets the PSC approve contributions in aid of construction and financial guarantees for large loads; FPL requires upfront payment for new facilities, but no specific collateral amounts found.
SB 484 bars utilities from shifting data center infrastructure costs to residential and small-business customers and requires large loads to bear full cost of service.
No statewide or confirmed local moratorium found; SB 484 expressly keeps local governments' zoning authority (they can deny projects).
pending: Local moratoria not searched exhaustively.

evidence: SB 484 leaves siting to local comprehensive planning and zoning (with local power to deny), treats large loads as non-substations, and requires a hearing before water consumptive-use permits for large data centers.
SB 484 defines a 'large-scale data center' as a single site with anticipated peak load of 50 MW or more, triggering special water-permit and tariff rules.
No fast-track or documented backlog for data center permits found; modifications by large data centers are processed like new applications.

Florida exempts qualifying data center property from sales tax only for facilities of 100 MW or more with at least $150 million invested and DOR certification (2025 HB 7031 raised the threshold from 15 MW).
pending: DOR guidance on applying the 100 MW threshold to existing certificate holders not yet issued.

evidence: No state data center property-tax abatement program found; SB 484 does not add one.

Sales-tax exemption requires DOR certificates, engineer and CPA certifications, and a five-year review, but no explicit clawback found; SB 484 adds public disclosure of data center agreements after a confidentiality period.
SB 484 requires reclaimed water where available, a conservation plan for applications of 100,000 gpd or more, and a hearing before consumptive-use permits; it does not set hard caps.
SB 484 does not address generator or air permitting; no Florida-specific data center generator limits found.
No data-center-specific state environmental review found beyond the water-permit conditions scored under ev_water.
SB 484 prohibits tariffs that hinder curtailment of service for grid stability, outage reduction or public safety; no mandatory demand-response requirement found.
No labor mandate for data centers found.
SB 484 requires public disclosure of data center development agreements after an initial exemption period and orders an OPPAGA study by July 1, 2027, but no recurring operator reporting.
No statewide noise or setback rules for data centers found.
The new law's tariff compliance is still under PSC review, DOR rule 12A-1.108 has not been updated to the 100 MW threshold, and an OPPAGA study due July 2027 may prompt further legislation.
pending: OPPAGA report July 2027; PSC action on utility tariffs.

evidence: No documented interconnection queue or agency backlog specific to data centers found.

Santee Cooper adopted a large-load rate (50 MW+, 15-year contract, four-year experimental) and Central Electric Power Cooperative approved a 20 MW+ rate in March 2026; Duke and Dominion apply large-load terms through contracts reviewed by the PSC.
pending: S.867 would direct the PSC to require data centers to cover full generation and transmission costs.

evidence: Duke Energy in SC reportedly requires 15-year terms with 75% take-or-pay, Dominion about 14 years with minimum bills and termination fees, and Central co-ops 15-year contracts with minimum monthly demand charges.

Utilities told a legislative subcommittee that Duke requires upfront transmission-upgrade deposits of roughly $20-130 million and that Santee Cooper and the co-ops require upfront security and cash deposits.
No SC statute mandates data centers pay their grid costs; protections come from utility tariffs/contracts under PSC prudency review, while S.867 (PSC full-cost mandate) and S.902 are pending.
pending: S.867 passed committee April 28, 2026 but was still in the Senate; session ended May 2026 with no sign of enactment.

evidence: House bill H.5286 proposes a statewide data center moratorium, and the Senate budget version includes a proviso temporarily halting Coordinating Council incentives for data centers; neither is shown as enacted.
pending: H.5286 and budget proviso status after May 2026 not confirmed.

evidence: Siting is currently by county zoning; S.867 would instead create a state permit through a new Data Center Development Office but has not been enacted.
pending: S.867 would replace county authority with a state siting permit.

evidence: No enacted state size threshold; S.867 would have tiered review at 1-10 MW, 11-50 MW and over 50 MW.
pending: S.867 tiered thresholds, if enacted, would score 100.

evidence: No fast-track or documented backlog; S.867 would set 60/90/120-day review clocks if enacted.
SC exempts data center computer equipment and electricity from sales tax; the exemptions cost the state about $828,000 last year per the Department of Revenue, and bills (S.784) would eliminate them.
pending: S.784 (Sen. Massey) would end blanket sales tax exemptions.

evidence: Searched but could not confirm whether SC data centers rely on state-authorized property-tax abatements (e.g., fee-in-lieu) as a routine program; budget-proviso study of data center tax exemptions was proposed.
Senate budget version would study tax exemption money going to data centers and pause Coordinating Council incentives; existing exemptions have limited stated conditions in sources found.
No enacted data center water limit or reporting found; the Senate budget version proposed a water-use reporting proviso due January 31, 2027 and S.867 would add annual reports.
pending: Senate budget proviso and S.867 water reporting not confirmed enacted.

evidence: No SC-specific generator rules for data centers found.
No data-center-specific state environmental review in place; S.867 would add site suitability and water assessments for 50 MW+ sites.
Duke Energy's SC large-load terms impose mandatory curtailment of 50-100 hours a year and the Central co-op rate lets co-ops cut power during shortages.
No labor condition on data centers found.
No enacted operating reporting requirement found; S.867 would require annual water and efficiency reporting.
No enacted statewide noise or setback rules; S.867 would add light, vibration and sound limits.
Multiple competing bills (S.867, S.784, S.902, H.5286) and budget provisos remain unresolved and the PSC and legislature are still defining large-load rules.
pending: S.867 and others carry over to the next session if not enacted.

evidence: Utilities reported data center proposals declining in SC; no documented backlog found.
Duke Energy, the Public Staff and others reached an October 2026 settlement on separate rates for customers using 50 MW+ at 80% load factor, awaiting NC Utilities Commission approval.
pending: NCUC approval of settlement; AG seeks separate class in Duke Energy Progress territory.

evidence: The settlement is described as imposing strict contract terms, and Duke's framework includes termination charges, but specific minimum-bill percentages and terms were not found.
pending: Terms depend on NCUC-approved tariff; SB 730 would require 15-year contracts above 100 MW.

evidence: Duke's Customer Protection Plus framework contemplates upfront financial security and customer-funded connection costs; this is a voluntary pledge pending a binding tariff.
pending: Gov. Stein and AG Jackson want these terms made enforceable through the NCUC.

evidence: Duke joined the federal Ratepayer Protection Pledge in July 2026 (voluntary), and SB 730 (Ratepayer Protection Act) passed the House but remains stalled in Senate Rules.
pending: SB 730 enactment or NCUC tariff approval would raise this to 100.

evidence: No statewide moratorium or proposal found, and I could not verify local moratoria in NC.
No state siting board; siting is local, though SB 730 would add noise analysis within 500 feet of property lines.
pending: SB 730 pending.

evidence: No enacted state review threshold; SB 730 uses 100 MW and Duke's tariff uses 50 MW as utility thresholds.
pending: SB 730 100 MW threshold pending.

evidence: No documented fast-track program or backlog for data center permits found.
The 2026 budget (S.L. 2026-41) repealed the sales-tax exemption for electricity used at certified data centers effective July 7, 2026, while other certified-datacenter exemptions remain.
pending: Gov. Stein proposed phasing out remaining data center incentives by 2033.

evidence: No state property-tax restriction in force; local economic development incentives remain available, though SB 730 would bar local incentives such as property-tax breaks.
pending: SB 730 ban on local incentives pending.

evidence: Certified-datacenter exemptions require state certification and S.L. 2026-42 adds quarterly reporting by electricity purchasers, but no explicit clawbacks found.
No enacted data center water limits; SB 730 would require closed-loop cooling for large data centers.
pending: SB 730 closed-loop cooling mandate pending.

evidence: No NC-specific data center generator rules found.
No data-center-specific state environmental review found.
Duke's framework allows curtailment of large loads during emergencies as part of voluntary long-term agreements; Gov. Stein also wants a program letting data centers bring their own generation.
No labor mandate for data centers found.
S.L. 2026-42 requires quarterly reporting by purchasers of electricity used at certified data centers, first report due October 30, 2026.
No statewide operating restrictions in force; SB 730 would require noise analysis near property lines.
pending: SB 730 pending.

evidence: SB 730 is pending in the Senate, the Duke settlement awaits NCUC approval, and Gov. Stein proposes phasing out incentives by 2033.
pending: NCUC order; SB 730 in Senate Rules.

evidence: No documented interconnection or agency backlog for data centers found in sources.

The PSC approved East Kentucky Power Cooperative's Data Center Power tariff (15 MW+, extra terms above 250 MW) in Case 2025-00140 on Oct. 30, 2025, and LG&E/KU publish an approved Extremely High Load Factor service rate.
pending: Status of Kentucky Power and Duke Energy Kentucky large-load tariffs not confirmed.

evidence: LG&E/KU sought an EHLF tariff requiring 15-year contracts and payment for at least 80% of forecast monthly energy; the utility now describes the rate as approved with long-term commitments.
pending: Approval order and final terms not verified from the PSC docket.

evidence: The EKPC tariff raised collateral requirements scaled to load plus application fees, and LG&E/KU's EHLF requires customers to pay full interconnection study costs before studies begin.

A bill (HB 593) requiring data centers to cover grid costs passed the House 90-8 but was stripped from SB 197 and died on the session's last day; cost protection exists only through PSC-approved utility tariffs.
pending: Senate President Stivers and Rep. Bray plan to revisit before the 2027 session.

evidence: No statewide or confirmed local moratorium found.
Siting is by local zoning; the PSC would not approve new generation until zoning and environmental permits are in place, but no state data center siting regime exists.
No enacted state size threshold for extra review; the failed HB 593 provisions (including a $75,000 application fee) were removed.
No fast-track program or documented permit backlog found.

Kentucky's 2025 data center law (HB 775, expanding the 2024 program) exempts data center equipment from sales and use tax for up to 50 years, with minimum investments of $25M to $450M depending on county population.
pending: Legislators (Stivers) champion the break; no repeal effort found.

evidence: No state-level restriction on property-tax incentives found; local abatements (e.g., industrial revenue bonds) were not verified.

The exemption requires the owner or colocation tenant to meet the minimum investment within five years of preliminary approval, but I found no clawback; a proposal tying tax breaks to local-rule compliance was stripped from the 2026 bill.

Ratepayer-protection legislation died in 2026 but is expected back in 2027 and the PSC is still shaping large-load tariffs.
